extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, damages experts, and patent attorneys handling infringement damages
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and practical rules for calculating and litigating reasonable royalty damages in patent infringement cases, including Georgia‑Pacific factors, hypothetical negotiation timing, apportionment rules, use of comparable licenses/benchmarks, and admissibility of survey evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Established royalty as simplest basis
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest way to determine a reasonable royalty is an established royalty, if one exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established royalties are the exception rather than the rule; most cases rely on alternative methods (e.g., Georgia‑Pacific factors or analytic approaches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well‑known fifteen‑factor framework courts commonly reference when setting a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Georgia‑Pacific factors are frequently considered by parties and damages experts, but the Federal Circuit has stated they are not an exclusive test and inapplicable factors should not be presented to a jury (doing so can be reversible error).

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (1) — Established royalties received by the patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: The royalties received by the patentee for the licensing of the patent in suit, proving or tending to prove an established royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider prior licensing income as direct evidence of an established royalty when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (2) — Rates paid for comparable patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The rates paid by the licensee for the use of other patents comparable to the patent in suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires showing comparability; courts scrutinize comparability and may exclude unrelated licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (3) — Nature and scope of the license
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and scope of the license, as exclusive or non‑exclusive; or as restricted or non‑restricted in terms of territory or with respect to whom the manufactured product may be sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess exclusivity, territory, field restrictions and how they affect royalty value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (4) — Licensor’s policy/marketing to maintain monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: The licensor’s established policy and marketing program to maintain his patent monopoly by not licensing others to use the invention or by granting licenses under special conditions designed to preserve that monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider patentee’s licensing strategy and its effect on license value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (5) — Commercial relationship between licensor and licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial relationship between the licensor and licensee, such as, whether they are competitors in the same territory in the same line of business; or whether they are inventor and promotor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine relationships (competitors, vertical relationships) that might alter negotiating positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (6) — Effect on sales of other products (convoyed sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of selling the patented specialty in promoting sales of other products of the licensee; the existing value of the invention to the licensor as a generator of sales of his non‑patented items; and the extent of such derivative or convoyed sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the patented feature drives additional sales of other items and how to value that effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (7) — Duration of the patent and term of the license
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of the patent and the term of the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider remaining patent life and contemplated license term when valuing royalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (8) — Established profitability, commercial success, popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: The established profitability of the product made under the patent; its commercial success; and its current popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence of commercial success as indicia of value, but ensure linkage to the patented features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (9) — Utility/advantages over prior modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The utility and advantages of the patent property over the old modes or devices, if any, that had been used for working out similar results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare patented invention to prior art and quantify advantages relevant to value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (10) — Nature and commercial embodiment of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of the patented invention; the character of the commercial embodiment of it as owned and produced by the licensor; and the benefits to those who have used the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how the invention is embodied in commerce and benefits end users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (11) — Extent of infringer’s use and probative evidence of that use
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the infringer has made use of the invention; and any evidence probative of the value of that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify infringing uses and link use intensity to value; surveys and usage metrics can be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (12) — Customary portion of profit or selling price
rubrics_metrics.description: The portion of the profit or of the selling price that may be customary in the particular business or in comparable businesses to allow for the use of the invention or analogous inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to industry norms for customary royalty percentages but justify comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (13) — Portion of realizable profit attributable to the invention (apportionment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The portion of the realizable profit that should be credited to the invention as distinguished from non‑patented elements, the manufacturing process, business risks, or significant features or improvements added by the infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportion profits to the patented contribution; avoid attributing value to non‑patented features (entire market value concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (14) — Opinion testimony of qualified experts
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion testimony of qualified experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts should apply reliable methodology, address applicability of factors, and avoid inadmissible or misleading evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factor (15) — Hypothetical negotiation/license (willing licensor/licensee)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount that a licensor and a licensee would have agreed upon (at the time the infringement began) if both had been reasonably and voluntarily trying to reach an agreement; i.e., what a prudent licensee would pay and a prudent patentee would accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core hypothetical negotiation construct; date and information available at that date are critical to its application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors are not exclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit has articulated that the Georgia‑Pacific factors are not an exclusive test for reasonable royalty calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court views Georgia‑Pacific as a list of admissible factors to inform reliable economic analysis; experts may use other sound methods (e.g., analytic approach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not instruct juries on inapplicable Georgia‑Pacific factors
rubrics_metrics.description: It is reversible error to instruct the jury on Georgia‑Pacific factors that are inapplicable to the facts of a particular case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages experts should discuss each factor, state whether it applies, and explain influence; parties should avoid reciting all fifteen factors in jury instructions regardless of applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic approach alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable royalty damages may be determined using the analytic approach, which calculates damages based on the infringer’s internal profit projections for the infringing item at the time the infringement began and then apportions the projected profit between the parties as a percentage of sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when internal projections exist and can be apportioned reliably; must relate to information available at the hypothetical negotiation date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select hypothetical negotiation date — set just before infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is ascertaining the date of the parties’ hypothetical negotiation, which should be set on a date just before infringement began and not influenced by anything other than the date of first infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct date is essential; even a one‑year difference can drastically alter expected risks and values (e.g., regulatory approvals). Statutes of limitations do not control selection of the negotiation date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book of wisdom doctrine — limited use of post‑negotiation events
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts sometimes allow reference to facts and events occurring after the hypothetical negotiation date to inform value (the 'book of wisdom'), but only if such subsequent events are closely related to the value of the patent at the time of first infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use post‑infringement evidence to correct uncertainty only to the extent it reveals elements of value that were present from the beginning; courts limit such evidence and require close relation to what parties would have known or expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire Market Value Rule (EMVR)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patented invention drives demand for the entire end product, a patentee may rely on the end product’s market value as the royalty base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EMVR applies only when the patented feature is the driver of demand for the whole product (common in pharmaceuticals); otherwise, using the entire product risks overcompensation and misleading the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallest Salable Patent‑Practicing Unit (SSPPU) principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent covers only a component of a multi‑component product, damages models that apportion from a royalty base should use the smallest salable patent‑practicing unit as the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justified to avoid compensating for non‑infringing components and to prevent skewing the jury by emphasizing total product revenue. SSPPU is the baseline; further apportionment may still be required if the smallest salable unit contains significant unpatented features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment beyond SSPPU when unpatented features remain
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee’s obligation to apportion damages only to the patented features does not end with identification of the smallest salable unit if that unit still contains significant unpatented features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts expect reasonable apportionment (not absolute precision); experts must separate value attributable to patented features from other value in the unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable license admissibility and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: To be admissible, any prior licensing agreement must involve technology that is closely comparable to the patent in suit; the party offering the license bears the burden of proving comparability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will exclude licenses lacking a discernible link to the claimed technology (e.g., ResQNet); comparability analysis must connect the license to the patented technology and market demand for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution when using settlement agreements as comparables
rubrics_metrics.description: Settlement agreements reached during litigation can skew the hypothetical negotiation and their propriety is questionable; there is no per se rule barring them but context matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement evidence may be admissible in some circumstances (e.g., where validity and infringement are assumed), but courts instruct district courts to consider such agreements in proper context and beware of litigation‑influenced pricing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark/comparable products
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts may use comparable or 'benchmark' products to inform reasonable royalty calculations, provided the benchmark is comparable to the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodology should identify comparable features, discount for non‑patented features, and justify valuation (examples: Apple Magic Trackpad used to value touch input features).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of consumer surveys to prove frequency of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer surveys can be used to show how frequently consumers use a particular feature of a multi‑component product (e.g., use rates for an infringing feature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys must be well designed (random sampling, proper screening questions to identify relevant respondents). Courts have accepted surveys for estimating number of infringing uses (e.g., i4i). Be cautious about assumptions for nonrespondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conjoint surveys to estimate willingness to pay (market value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjoint surveys attempt to quantify customer preferences for product attributes to estimate the market’s willingness to pay for a patented feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepted in high‑stakes cases if properly designed; typical two‑phase approach: (1) identify a limited set (≤6) of comparable attributes, (2) present hypothetical bundles with price variations to elicit tradeoffs, then analyze with industry‑standard software. Courts have both admitted and excluded conjoint surveys depending on reliability and design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey design best practices (as illustrated by case law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepted conjoint/survey methods include phase‑one attribute prioritization to select ~6 comparable attributes, followed by phase‑two choice tasks with price discounts to estimate value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit attributes to six or fewer; use screening to identify appropriate respondents; test accused feature against non‑infringing alternatives; analyze using industry‑standard tools; document assumptions (e.g., treatment of nonrespondents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of actual infringer profits — limited admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of the infringer’s actual profits generally is admissible as probative of expected/anticipated profits, but only in an indirect and limited way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual profits may inform anticipated profits at the negotiation date, but courts caution against substituting after‑the‑fact profits for what parties would have known at the hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology/admissibility requirement for expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony must apply sound methodology, tie to facts, and address comparability and apportionment; unreliable methodology can lead to exclusion or reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: improperly using unrelated licenses or emphasizing whole‑product revenue without apportionment can lead to vacatur or new trial (e.g., Uniloc). Experts should explain applicability of Georgia‑Pacific factors and limitations.
